blocks.text: You are a junior doctor in a gynaecology clinic. A 29-year-old woman presents with her husband because they have been trying to conceive for two years without success.

items.text: Take a focused history.
Explain the possible causes of infertility.
Outline the initial investigations for both partners.
Discuss the initial management plan.

blocks.text: Possible alternative stations

items.text: A 25-year-old woman who has never conceived despite regular unprotected intercourse.
A woman with irregular menstrual cycles and difficulty conceiving.
A couple who are anxious about their inability to have a child.
A consultation requiring you to interpret infertility investigation results.

blocks.text: Primary infertility is the inability to achieve a pregnancy after a specified period of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse in a woman who has never previously achieved a pregnancy.

blocks.title: In many clinical guidelines, infertility is evaluated after:

items.text: 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse when the female partner is younger than 35 years.
6 months when the female partner is aged 35 years or older.
Earlier assessment when there are risk factors such as amenorrhoea, markedly irregular cycles, known tubal disease, endometriosis, or suspected male-factor infertility.

blocks.text: Some definitions and referral thresholds vary between guidelines and clinical settings. In practice, do not delay assessment when a clear risk factor is present.

rows: Failure to conceive for the first time
Similar causes, including newly acquired disease

blocks.text: OSCE tip: Do not confuse primary infertility with primary amenorrhoea. A woman with primary infertility may menstruate regularly and have no obvious symptoms.
Start the station professionally and non-judgmentally.

items.text: Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm the patient's identity and preferred name.
Ensure privacy and establish a comfortable environment.
Explain that you would like to ask questions about both partners' reproductive and sexual health.
Obtain consent before beginning.
Ask whether the patient would prefer to speak alone initially or have her partner present.
Use inclusive, respectful language and avoid assigning blame.

blocks.text: “Hello, my name is …, and I am one of the doctors in the gynaecology clinic. I understand that you have been trying to conceive without success. I appreciate that this can be a stressful experience. I would like to ask you some questions about your menstrual cycles, previous pregnancies, medical history and both partners' reproductive health so that we can identify possible causes and plan appropriate investigations. Is that alright with you?”
Important: Infertility is a couple-level clinical problem. Avoid assuming that the cause is female simply because the woman is attending the clinic.
The aim is to identify whether the problem is related to ovulation, the fallopian tubes, the uterus, sperm production or function, sexual factors, or a combination of causes.
Use a systematic approach rather than asking random questions.

content_groups.group_title: A. History of the presenting complaint

items.text: How long have you been trying to conceive?
When did you stop using contraception?
How often do you have sexual intercourse?
Do you have intercourse throughout the menstrual cycle or only around ovulation?
Have you ever had a positive pregnancy test?
Have you or your partner ever had a fertility assessment?
Are there any known reproductive problems in either partner?

blocks.text: Interpretation of answers

rows: Trying for 2 years with regular intercourse
Meets the usual definition of infertility
Intercourse infrequently or with prolonged gaps
Never had a positive pregnancy test
Supports primary infertility as described in the history
Previous positive pregnancy test, miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy
Clarify whether the history is actually secondary infertility
Known endometriosis or previous pelvic infection
Male partner has previous testicular surgery

blocks.text: Remember to clarify sexual frequency sensitively. Intercourse every 2–3 days throughout the cycle generally provides good coverage of the fertile window.
This is one of the most important components because it helps assess ovulatory function.

items.text: Age at menarche.
First day of the last menstrual period.
Cycle length.
Cycle regularity.
Duration and volume of bleeding.
Dysmenorrhoea.
Intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.
Amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea.
Symptoms of premenstrual changes, where relevant.

blocks.text: **Interpreting menstrual patterns**
Regular cycles
Predictable cycles commonly suggest ovulation, although they do not prove that ovulation occurs in every cycle or establish tubal patency.
Oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea
Suggests possible ovulatory dysfunction. Causes include polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid dysfunction, hypothalamic dysfunction and primary ovarian insufficiency.
Severe dysmenorrhoea
Raises suspicion of endometriosis, adenomyosis or other pelvic pathology, particularly when associated with deep dyspareunia or chronic pelvic pain.
Very scanty menstruation or absent periods after uterine instrumentation
May suggest intrauterine adhesions, particularly following dilatation and curettage or other uterine procedures.

OSCE pearl: Ask about cycle regularity before immediately ordering hormonal tests. In a woman with regular cycles, routine confirmation of ovulation may not always be necessary, depending on the guideline and clinical context.
Ask specifically about previous pregnancies, even if the patient says she has never delivered.

items.text: Have you ever been pregnant?
Have you ever had a miscarriage or termination of pregnancy?
Have you ever had an ectopic pregnancy?
Have you had a molar pregnancy?
Have you undergone any uterine evacuation or other pregnancy-related procedure?

blocks.text: A woman who has never achieved a pregnancy has primary infertility. Previous pregnancy followed by difficulty conceiving again is secondary infertility, even if the previous pregnancy did not result in a live birth, subject to the definition being used.

items.text: Previous pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).
Previous sexually transmitted infections, particularly chlamydia and gonorrhoea.
Endometriosis.
Fibroids, especially those distorting the uterine cavity.
Ovarian cysts or previous ovarian surgery.
Previous pelvic or abdominal surgery.
Tuberculosis exposure or previous genital tuberculosis where epidemiologically relevant.
Cervical procedures or uterine instrumentation.
Abnormal cervical screening results where relevant.

blocks.text: Clinical reasoning: Previous PID, ectopic pregnancy and pelvic surgery increase concern for tubal damage or pelvic adhesions. However, the absence of symptoms does not exclude tubal disease.
Ask about features that may suggest an underlying hormonal cause.

rows: PCOS or another cause of androgen excess
Hyperprolactinaemia, medication effect or other pituitary pathology
Hot flushes, vaginal dryness and amenorrhoea
Marked weight loss, excessive exercise or restrictive eating
Headache or visual disturbance with amenorrhoea or galactorrhoea

blocks.text: Do not diagnose an endocrine disorder from symptoms alone; use the clinical context and appropriate investigations.

items.text: How often do you have intercourse?
Is intercourse painful?
Does either partner have difficulty with erection or ejaculation?
Is ejaculation intravaginal?
Is there reduced libido?
Are there vaginal dryness or penetration difficulties?
Do either of you have concerns about sexual performance?

blocks.text: These questions identify potentially treatable barriers to conception. Offer privacy when discussing sensitive matters.

items.text: Diabetes mellitus.
Thyroid disease.
Renal or hepatic disease.
Autoimmune disorders.
Previous chemotherapy or radiotherapy.
Previous pelvic, abdominal, testicular or reproductive surgery.
Medications that may affect reproductive function.
Allergies and previous anaesthetic complications, particularly if procedures are anticipated.

content_groups.group_title: H. Drug, lifestyle and family history

items.text: Smoking, alcohol and recreational drug use.
Body weight changes, diet and exercise.
Occupational exposure to heat, toxins or radiation.
Previous use of anabolic steroids by the male partner.
Testosterone treatment in the male partner, which can suppress sperm production.
Family history of early menopause, infertility, genetic disorders or recurrent pregnancy loss.

blocks.text: Never omit the male partner's assessment. Male factors contribute to a substantial proportion of infertility cases, either alone or alongside female factors.

items.text: Previous pregnancies with any partner.
Previous semen analysis or fertility treatment.
Childhood mumps orchitis.
Undescended testes.
Testicular trauma, torsion or surgery.
Genital infections, including sexually transmitted infections.
Erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction.
Previous vasectomy.
Chemotherapy or radiotherapy.
Medication use, including testosterone and anabolic steroids.
Smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs and occupational exposures.

blocks.text: A normal sexual history does not guarantee normal sperm production.
Ask how infertility is affecting the couple.

items.text: How has this experience affected you emotionally?
Has it affected your relationship?
Is either partner experiencing pressure from family or the community?
What are your expectations regarding treatment?
Are there financial, cultural or religious concerns you would like us to consider?

blocks.text: Provide reassurance without making promises about pregnancy. Do not assume that the couple wants IVF or that they would accept donor gametes or adoption.
In a history-taking-only station, explain which examinations may be appropriate and why. In a combined assessment station, proceed with consent and chaperoning as indicated.

items.text: Assess general appearance and vital signs as clinically indicated.
Measure height, weight and calculate BMI.
Look for hirsutism, acne and androgenic hair loss.
Look for signs of thyroid disease.
Assess for galactorrhoea only when indicated and with consent.
Look for features suggesting hypo-oestrogenism or systemic disease.

blocks.title: With consent and appropriate exposure, assess for:

items.text: Abdominal masses.
Previous surgical scars.
Tenderness.
Organ enlargement or other relevant pathology.

blocks.text: A pelvic examination is not automatically necessary in every initial infertility consultation. Perform it when indicated by symptoms, history or the planned investigation, with informed consent and a chaperone according to local practice.

items.text: Cervical discharge or signs of infection.
Cervical stenosis.
Uterine enlargement or irregularity due to fibroids.
Adnexal masses.
Pelvic tenderness or reduced organ mobility, which may suggest endometriosis or adhesions.

blocks.text: A normal examination does not exclude tubal obstruction, endometriosis, ovulatory dysfunction or male-factor infertility.

subsections.subsection_title: 6. Normal and abnormal findings: how to interpret them

blocks.text: This is where you demonstrate clinical reasoning rather than merely listing symptoms.

rows: Normal ovulatory function, though not guaranteed
Previous uterine evacuation followed by scanty periods
No sperm detected in the ejaculate
Obstructive or non-obstructive causes, among others
Multiple testicular, endocrine or other causes
Normal initial assessment of both partners
No cause may be identified initially
Possible unexplained infertility after appropriate evaluation

blocks.text: Pattern 1: Suspected PCOS
A 27-year-old woman has been trying to conceive for 18 months. Her cycles occur every 2–3 months, and she has facial hair and acne.
Interpretation: Ovulatory dysfunction is likely. Assess for PCOS and other causes of irregular menstruation.
Pattern 2: Suspected tubal-factor infertility
A 30-year-old woman has regular cycles but a history of PID.
Interpretation: Ovulation may be occurring, but tubal obstruction or damage is possible. Tubal patency assessment is important.
Pattern 3: Suspected male-factor infertility
A couple has tried to conceive for two years. The woman has regular cycles, but her partner previously underwent surgery for undescended testes.
Interpretation: Investigate both partners, with particular attention to semen analysis and male reproductive assessment.
Pattern 4: Possible unexplained infertility
Both partners have no obvious risk factors, and initial testing is reassuring.
Interpretation: Complete an appropriate fertility assessment before classifying the problem as unexplained infertility.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to report the history and examination

blocks.text: In an OSCE, your report should summarise the duration, relevant risk factors, likely mechanism and proposed next steps.

content_groups.group_title: Example 1: Primary infertility with suspected ovulatory dysfunction

blocks.text: “This is a 27-year-old woman presenting with 18 months of primary infertility. She reports infrequent, irregular menstruation and symptoms of androgen excess. These findings suggest ovulatory dysfunction, with PCOS among the leading differential diagnoses. I would assess for alternative endocrine causes, arrange appropriate ovulatory and metabolic investigations, obtain a semen analysis from her partner and assess tubal patency as indicated.”

content_groups.group_title: Example 2: Primary infertility with suspected tubal disease

blocks.text: “This is a 30-year-old woman presenting with two years of primary infertility. Her menstrual cycles are regular, but she has a history of pelvic inflammatory disease. Although ovulation is likely, tubal-factor infertility is a concern. I would arrange assessment of tubal patency, evaluate her partner with semen analysis and investigate further according to the findings.”

content_groups.group_title: Example 3: Primary infertility with possible male factor

blocks.text: “This couple presents with two years of primary infertility. The woman reports regular menstrual cycles and has no obvious history suggestive of pelvic disease. Her partner has a history of testicular surgery. Male-factor infertility must be considered, and I would arrange semen analysis and appropriate male reproductive assessment while completing the woman's evaluation.”

“This couple presents with primary infertility despite regular unprotected intercourse. The initial history does not identify an obvious cause. I would investigate both partners, assess ovulatory function where indicated, establish tubal patency and evaluate semen parameters before considering unexplained infertility.”
Examiner tip: Avoid stating that the woman is fertile merely because she menstruates regularly, or that the man is fertile because he has normal sexual function.

subsections.subsection_title: 8. Differential diagnoses and causes of primary infertility

blocks.text: Use the framework MOTUS to remember the main categories.
M — Male factor
Abnormal sperm production, impaired motility, obstruction, ejaculation disorders or sexual dysfunction.
O — Ovulatory disorders
PCOS, thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinaemia, hypothalamic dysfunction and primary ovarian insufficiency.
T — Tubal and pelvic factors
Tubal obstruction, previous PID, pelvic adhesions and endometriosis.
U — Uterine and cervical factors
Cavity-distorting fibroids, endometrial polyps, intrauterine adhesions and selected cervical abnormalities.
S — Sexual, unexplained and other factors
Infrequent intercourse, sexual dysfunction, age-related decline in fertility and unexplained infertility after an appropriate work-up.
Remember that more than one factor can coexist. For example, a woman may have both PCOS and tubal damage, while her partner may also have reduced sperm motility.
The key principle is to investigate both partners in parallel, tailoring the tests to the history and examination rather than ordering every available investigation indiscriminately.

content_groups.group_title: A. Investigations in the female partner

blocks.text: 1. Ovulation assessment

items.text: Menstrual history is the initial assessment.
Serum progesterone can be measured approximately seven days before the expected next menstrual period when confirmation of ovulation is needed.
Do not automatically order progesterone on day 21 for every woman; that timing is appropriate only for a cycle of approximately 28 days.
If cycles are irregular, time testing to the expected next period where possible or investigate the underlying cause of ovulatory dysfunction.

blocks.text: 2. Hormonal investigations

rows: Consider when ovarian insufficiency or another cause of amenorrhoea is suspected; interpret together and in clinical context
Assess when thyroid dysfunction is suspected or according to local infertility guidance
Particularly indicated with galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea
Consider with hirsutism, acne or other signs of androgen excess
May help estimate ovarian reserve and predict response to ovarian stimulation; it does not reliably predict spontaneous conception on its own

blocks.text: Important distinction: Ovarian reserve tests help guide treatment planning. They do not independently establish whether a woman can conceive naturally.
3. Pelvic ultrasound

blocks.title: Transvaginal ultrasound, when appropriate and acceptable, can assess:

items.text: Uterine anatomy and endometrial appearance.
Fibroids and possible cavity distortion.
Ovarian morphology and adnexal masses.
Antral follicle count when relevant to ovarian reserve assessment.
Features suggestive of endometriosis or other pelvic pathology.

blocks.text: A normal ultrasound does not exclude tubal obstruction or all forms of endometriosis.
4. Tubal patency assessment

items.text: Hysterosalpingography (HSG): Contrast radiography used to assess the uterine cavity and whether the fallopian tubes appear patent.
HyCoSy: Ultrasound-based assessment of tubal patency using contrast.

Laparoscopy with chromopertubation: May be appropriate when there is suspected pelvic pathology, endometriosis or another indication for surgery; it is not routinely required for every infertility patient.

blocks.text: Before tubal testing, assess for pregnancy and active genital tract infection, and follow local procedural protocols.
5. Additional investigations when indicated

items.text: Hysteroscopy for suspected intrauterine adhesions, polyps or cavity pathology.
Further assessment of a uterine abnormality identified on imaging.
Infection testing based on symptoms, history and planned procedures.
Genetic or autoimmune investigations only when clinically indicated.

blocks.text: Routine diagnostic laparoscopy, endometrial biopsy to confirm ovulation and broad, indiscriminate thrombophilia or immune testing are not standard investigations for every couple with infertility.

content_groups.group_title: B. Investigations in the male partner

blocks.text: Semen analysis is a first-line investigation.

items.text: Semen volume.
Sperm concentration and total sperm number.
Sperm motility.
Sperm morphology.
Other laboratory parameters according to the laboratory protocol.

blocks.text: An abnormal result should be interpreted against the laboratory's reference standards and the clinical context. Repeat testing is often appropriate because semen parameters vary between samples.

items.text: Reproductive hormone tests, such as FSH and morning testosterone, when indicated.
Examination by a clinician experienced in male reproductive health.
Scrotal ultrasound for selected clinical indications.
Genetic testing in selected cases of severe sperm-production abnormalities or azoospermia.
Assessment for obstruction, infection or ejaculatory dysfunction where suspected.

blocks.text: Do not assume that a single abnormal semen analysis establishes permanent infertility.

rows: No ovulation on appropriately timed assessment
Review cycle history and endocrine causes
Confirm and assess causes, including medications and thyroid function
Integrate with the remaining fertility assessment
Specialist review; confirmatory assessment may be needed
Assess symptoms, location and reproductive implications
Repeat as appropriate and refer for male reproductive assessment
Confirm result and investigate obstructive versus non-obstructive causes
Consider unexplained infertility if the evaluation is complete

blocks.text: Management depends on the cause, the woman's age, duration of infertility, ovarian reserve where relevant, tubal status, semen parameters, previous treatment and the couple's preferences.

content_groups.group_title: Step 1: Explain the findings and agree on a plan

blocks.text: Begin by acknowledging the emotional impact, explaining that infertility is not necessarily anyone's fault, and emphasising that a treatable cause may be found.
Discuss the proposed investigations, their limitations, possible discomforts and costs. Provide an opportunity for questions and shared decision-making.

content_groups.group_title: Step 2: General measures to optimise fertility

items.text: Regular intercourse every 2–3 days.
Smoking cessation and avoidance of recreational drugs.
Avoiding excessive alcohol consumption.
Maintaining a balanced diet and a healthy weight.
Reviewing medications and occupational exposures.
Optimising chronic medical conditions before pregnancy.
Folic acid supplementation before conception, generally 400 micrograms daily for women at usual risk, with higher doses for specific indications under local guidance.

blocks.text: Avoid presenting lifestyle changes as a substitute for indicated fertility treatment.
A. Ovulatory dysfunction

Treat the underlying cause where possible. For anovulatory infertility due to PCOS without other infertility factors, letrozole is generally recommended as first-line pharmacological ovulation induction in appropriate patients. Check pregnancy status and assess for other relevant factors before treatment.
B. Tubal-factor infertility

Management depends on the site and severity of tubal disease, age, ovarian reserve and semen findings. Options may include selected surgical approaches or IVF. Significant bilateral tubal disease often makes IVF the more appropriate option.
C. Male-factor infertility

Address reversible causes where identified, review medications and refer for appropriate male reproductive assessment. Depending on the findings, treatment may involve correction of selected conditions, intrauterine insemination (IUI), IVF or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI).
D. Uterine or pelvic pathology

Consider treatment of selected cavity-distorting fibroids, endometrial polyps or intrauterine adhesions when the expected benefit outweighs the risks. Surgery for endometriosis should be individualised, especially when ovarian reserve may be affected.
E. Unexplained infertility

Management depends on age, duration of infertility, previous pregnancies and local guidance. Options include expectant management in selected couples, ovarian stimulation with IUI in appropriate settings, and IVF when indicated. Avoid indefinite empirical treatment without reassessing the plan.

blocks.title: Refer early to a fertility specialist when there is:

items.text: Female age 35 years or older with six months of unsuccessful attempts, or earlier where clinically indicated.
Female age over 40 years, for prompt assessment.
Amenorrhoea or marked menstrual irregularity.
Suspected tubal disease or significant endometriosis.
Severe male-factor infertility or azoospermia.
Suspected primary ovarian insufficiency.
Previous chemotherapy, radiotherapy or other major risk to reproductive function.
Prolonged infertility or unsuccessful initial management.

blocks.text: Referral thresholds vary by local service, so follow the applicable clinical pathway.

content_groups.group_title: Step 5: Discuss assisted reproductive options when appropriate

items.text: Ovulation induction: Medication used to induce ovulation in selected patients.
IUI: Prepared sperm is placed into the uterus around ovulation; it requires appropriate clinical circumstances and is not suitable for every type of infertility.
IVF: Eggs are collected, fertilised in the laboratory and an embryo is transferred to the uterus.
ICSI: A single sperm is injected into an egg during IVF, commonly used for selected cases of significant male-factor infertility or previous fertilisation failure.

blocks.text: Counsel about likely benefits, limitations, financial implications, emotional burden and treatment-specific risks. Never promise a successful pregnancy.
Agree on a review date to discuss results, explain the diagnosis and determine the next step. Provide support for distress and refer for counselling when helpful.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Questions the examiner may ask — with model answers

blocks.text: Q1. Define infertility.

Model answer: Infertility is a disease of the reproductive system characterised by failure to achieve pregnancy after 12 months or more of regular unprotected sexual intercourse. Earlier evaluation is appropriate when age or clinical risk factors warrant it.
Q2. What is primary infertility?
Model answer: Inability to achieve a pregnancy in someone who has never previously achieved a pregnancy, after an appropriate period of regular unprotected intercourse.
Q3. What are the major causes of infertility?

Model answer: Male factors, ovulatory disorders, tubal and pelvic disease, uterine or cervical factors, sexual factors, age-related decline and unexplained infertility. More than one cause may coexist.
Q4. Why must both partners be investigated?
Model answer: Infertility may be caused by the male partner, female partner or both. Assessing both partners early avoids missed diagnoses and unnecessary delays or invasive investigations.
Q5. What is the first-line investigation in the male partner?
Model answer: Semen analysis, with repeat testing when indicated by an abnormal result or the clinical context.
Q6. How do you assess ovulation?

Model answer: Begin with menstrual history. If confirmation is needed, measure serum progesterone at an appropriately timed point, usually about seven days before the expected next menstruation. Investigate irregular cycles for their underlying cause.
Q7. What is the role of AMH?

Model answer: Anti-Müllerian hormone can help estimate ovarian reserve and predict ovarian response during stimulation. It should not be used alone to determine whether a woman can conceive naturally.
Q8. How is tubal patency assessed?
Model answer: Hysterosalpingography or ultrasound-based contrast testing such as HyCoSy can assess tubal patency. Laparoscopy with chromopertubation is reserved for selected clinical indications.
Q9. What is unexplained infertility?

Model answer: Infertility in which the standard evaluation of ovulation, tubal patency and semen parameters has not identified a cause. It is a diagnosis made after an appropriate evaluation, not simply after normal menstrual cycles and a normal ultrasound.
Q10. What is the first-line drug for ovulation induction in PCOS-related anovulatory infertility?

Model answer: Letrozole is generally first-line in appropriate patients with PCOS-related anovulatory infertility when no other infertility factor has been identified. Treatment should be supervised, with attention to contraindications and pregnancy status.
Q11. What is the difference between IUI and IVF?
Model answer: IUI places prepared sperm into the uterus around ovulation, whereas IVF involves collecting eggs, fertilising them outside the body and transferring an embryo into the uterus.
Q12. How would you counsel a distressed couple?

Model answer: I would acknowledge their distress, explain that infertility is not necessarily anyone's fault, provide clear information about possible causes and investigations, involve both partners with consent, and agree on a supportive, individualised plan without promising an outcome.
These errors can cost marks even when your medical knowledge is good.
Investigating only the woman
Always assess both partners in parallel.
Assuming regular menstruation proves ovulation
Regular cycles make ovulation more likely but do not establish tubal patency or guarantee normal fertility.
Ordering progesterone on day 21 for everyone
Time the test in relation to the expected next period, not an arbitrary cycle day.
Ordering every hormonal test indiscriminately
Select investigations based on history, examination and applicable guidelines.
Failing to ask about sexual function
Erectile dysfunction, ejaculatory problems, painful intercourse and infrequent intercourse can affect conception.
Assuming an abnormal semen analysis means permanent infertility
Repeat testing and further assessment may be required.
Ignoring age and duration of infertility
These affect prognosis, referral urgency and treatment selection.
Blaming or stigmatising either partner
Maintain confidentiality, empathy and a non-judgmental approach.
